I had Claude write a style guide for coding Roc on my projects. I would love for a human to give it an adversarial review (even subjective things).

https://github.com/showell/roc-apps/blob/master/docs/roc-style.md

I tried to make the style guide fairly general, but it includes a few things specific to my workflow. Folks are welcome to fork this, and most of the Steve-specific stuff should be easy for an agent to remove.

Some tips for state machines:

  • State machines MUST be an opaque type.
  • A tag union that describes effects or state changes, MUST use verbs as tag e.g. instead of InsertMode(...) (describes what state is it) use SwitchToInsert(...) (describe what to do).

@notramo Thanks!

Style guide:

  • Main change: https://github.com/showell/roc-apps/commit/fc96a513e06a96271feb68ab19b574c9f0896b34
    • name a tag as a command, an event or a state;
    • a state machine is an opaque type whose module owns the transitions;
    • the last "(not yet settled)" removed.
  • Follow-up: https://github.com/showell/roc-apps/commit/0c0af39cc1697519a7e04cdadeba177744d2b712, adding the new check to the guide's enforcement list.

New Shale check: https://github.com/showell/shale/commit/0b59e5102dbd14bf06f978f72325619cd0b3d9a1

  • command_tense in name_hunt flags an effect that's told what to do in past tense: a tag union whose tags all read as done ([Pinned, Unpinned]), written in place or declared in any file.
  • Five plants: two that must fire, three that must stay quiet.
  • Red/green on real code: on the chat before my rename it flags pin! and write_pins!; after the rename, nothing.
  • A false positive caught before pushing. The first run on the chat flagged Who : [Known(…), Unasked] seven times. That's a state carried along, not an instruction. The check now skips any union where a tag carries data, and a plant holds that case.

Code changes: https://github.com/showell/roc-webbox/commit/692aa768ee83fc29809b5f8a222216330af9053a

  • ChatState.Pin : [Pinned, Unpinned] became PinEdit : [Pin
  • Fanout.Step's Feed(…) became AppendFeed(…).
  • The quick gate passes, with real tests including the pinn-out goldens.

I noticed that certain cheaper LLMs tend to underuse the pipe operator and methods, and nest the function calls instead. Add this:

  • Try to reduce the number of nested calls.
    • Method calls are the best.
    • Pipe operator |> is second.
    • If none of the above fits, nesting remains as a third option.
Some more:
• Vague container words are a smell. Entry, Item, Node, Data and Info usually stand in for a word the domain already has, or can be described in a more accurate word.

• Do not use optionals.
    For example, a parser.peek() should not return [Some(Str), None], but [Grapheme(Str), Eof].
    The Some doesn't say anything about what is in that Str, but a Grapheme says it.
    The None just specifies the lack of a value, Eof provides more info by also indicating the reason.
    See a more detailed explanation with examples: https://www.roc-lang.org/faq#option-type

• Reduce what a reader must remember to understand the code. Ask yourself: how many other definitions someone must read to know what a line does? Every jump to a helper, every hidden assumption, and every parameter that never varies adds to that count. A good name helps in this: the reader can figure out the behavior, or helps them remember it. With a bad name, the reader has to remember the implementation too, and also the exact name, since it's not obvious from the name. A rule of thumb: if a helper is used in one place and it's less than 3-4 ines of code, it probably should be inlined. If it largely depends on behavior elsewhere, it probably should be inlined instead.

• Local reasoning over fragmentation. A function boundary must earn its existence by naming a genuine domain concept, isolating platform fiddliness, or eliminating substantial repetition. Do not fracture a 10-line coherent linear flow into five 2-line helpers just because you can. Every helper introduces a name to remember and a call to jump to. And also ambiguity: most names don't accurately describe every behavior. If documenting the behavior would require more text than the function body, it's probably a bad idea to split it. If it's just repacking the error tags with different names, it's probably a bad idea.

• Do not define a shared error type. It's not Rust.
    Roc can infer the error tag union using the _ type variable: Try(..., _).
    Let the compiler infer the actually returned errors. Or specify them yourself one by one if you want to keep track of it, and prevent accidentally introducing more error tags than intended. So, no Try(Str, ParserError) but Try(Str, [Eof, UnexpectedChar])
    This is important so the caller don't have to handle all tags in a type, even if the function only returns a subset of those.

• Treat for and while loops as syntax sugar, not a way to structure code.
    Rule of thumb: if only one var $... is needed to implement a loop, it can provide a more concise code than e.g. a .fold(), especially if something is modified conditionally during the fold, so it would reqire adding a tag union for state tracking. Reduce the cognitive complexity of the code. An extra tag union, an extra variable (e.g. fold state) all add to the complexity.

Extend this rule:

  • Use a nominal type (:=) where values of the same shape mean different things. A name passed where an id belongs is then a type error (types).

I would add this sentence:

This is known as the "newtype pattern" in Rust, and Roc has excellent support for it.

• Name functions from the callee's perspective, not the caller's. I.e. name after what it does and not what it's used for. A tokenizer function checking if text starts with a letter should be has_alphanumeric_at(cursor), not starts_identifier(cursor). The caller knows the purpose: is checking the start of an identifier; the function only knows what it does: if an alphanumeric char is at the cursor.

I have a gist I've been periodically updating, I fed claude the above notes and pointed it at a some examples I had and updated it https://gist.github.com/lukewilliamboswell/241a4e8adb7c89c7e0e02f1d303a8fa1

Inline a helper that is used once and is under 3–4 lines, or that mostly depends on behaviour defined elsewhere.

I think most LLMs will get confused by this shorter definition. It's not always valid. It's a rule of thumb, not a hard rule. Just to make the bias a bit weaker, not to completely disable. It's mostly a workaround for weaker LLMs. An LLM that would not do it by default just gets confused by this, so I would recommend adding the longer explanation.

Use := where values of the same shape mean different things, so passing a name where an id belongs is a type error.

If you want it concise, simply add this to the end: (a.k.a. "newtype" pattern in Rust).
The "newtype" word probably would activate some Rust-related weights, that would benefit from the usage examples in the vast Rust training data, to help in deciding when to use it.

Some more rules:

  • If something is transformed multiple times, and method chaining/piping does not fit the use case, use a var $… instead of numbering, e.g. var $prng instead of prng0, prng1, prng2. A variable assignment overwrites the old value, so it can not be accidentally reused later. You can even declare variables in lambda parameter lists: |var $prng| ....

Does anyone have a preference to not use method syntax?

For example, comparing:

match messages.last() {
    ...
}

to

match List.last(messages) {
   ...
}

I have found agents to prefer the latter one. One benefit of the second one is that it's clear what type you are dealing with at a glance. :thinking:
I prefer the method style, mostly because it's shorter
I suppose it reads nicer too!

Reading it I think is clearer to, like putting the subject first in a sentence. To me it feels like "match on the last message" as opposed to "match on the last value in the list called messages". I don't know how well that holds up grammatically though

Static dispatch (and pipe chains) become even nicer when nested calls are involved, such as:

"Hello world!".split_on(" ") |> Str.join_with(", ")

With regular calls, it would look like this:

Str.join_with(Str.split_on("Hello world!", " "), ", ")

I have found agents to prefer the latter one.

I guess it's due to the majority of FP training data being from FP languages that don't have method syntax.
Isn't the method syntax fairly new even in Roc?

Most functions just take arguments and the user has to know or look up in the documentation, what each argument means, e.g. 

Str.replace_each : Str, Str, Str -> Str # first is input Str, second argument is delimiter, third replacement
expect "a,b,c".replace_each(",", " and ") == "a and b and c"

I personally prefer this kind of style, and it is fairly easy in roc:

replace_each : Str, { delimiter: Str, replacement: Str } -> Str
expect "a,b,c".replace_each({ delimiter: ",", replacement: " and " }) == "a and b and c"

it seems like the first one is basically the standard, what are your thoughts on the second API style?
Doesn't it add some overhead?

My style guide addresses the pitfall that Str, Str, Str -> Str doesn't give you enough semantic info with the following rule (and some other rules are also kinda relevant):

Neighbouring arguments of one type get a record, even when there are only two of them: they can be swapped and still type-check, and a record names the fields, so order can't go wrong: appended!(conv, who, draft), not four Strs in a row (records).
I prefer named arguments, and would like to see them in Roc, but usually it's not that big issue like in other languages.
I think removewingman is speaking to a slightly broader issue than I mentioned above, to be clear. My answer: I think there are cases where the more explicit style is worth it.
For example, when I write Zig or TypeScript functions, those have more arguments on average than Roc functions. I don't know why, maybe different code organization.

My biggest pet peeve is when my fellow humans write code like foo(true, false, true). I have seen this countless times. You have no idea what the booleans mean locally. Especially in JS, I got in the habit of just passing structs to almost every non-trivial function.
For bools, it's often better to name the choices, e.g. [Offline, Online] instead of [True, False]. So it's self-documenting, even without named params.
It's also possible in Zig with anonymous enums, and TypeScript with literal strings as types, e.g. 'online' | 'offline'.
Although the strings might cause some performance overhead, but if performance is important for a task, TypeScript is a quite bad choice anyways.

Cool! I asked Claude for a couple examples that you can point your agent at:

Shale is public on GitHub. From easiest to hardest:

  1. nest_depth.shale (160 lines): flags a call nested three deep, f(g(h(x))). It's one rule and a simple walk over Roc's parse tree.
    https://github.com/showell/shale/blob/master/cookbook/roc/nest_depth.shale

  2. errors.shale (312 lines): two error-style rules from the Roc style guide, an error alias where tags should be written out in place, and an optional value written as a tag. It has to follow type aliases and module types, so it reads the tree with more context.
    https://github.com/showell/shale/blob/master/cookbook/roc/errors.shale

  3. boundaries.shale (441 lines): finds every top-level and module-member function and every reference to it, and flags a parameter that is never used. This means resolving names across a file, so it's the closest of the three to real analysis.
    https://github.com/showell/shale/blob/master/cookbook/roc/boundaries.shale

Useful context for him:

  • Test cases: each recipe's planted examples are in https://github.com/showell/shale/tree/master/cookbook/roc/plants. The good-and-bad files there make a ready-made test suite for a Roc port.
  • What they parse with: all three read Roc's own parser output through roc-ast. nest_depth uses Shale's newer roc_tree builtin; the other two parse roc-ast's text dump directly. A native Roc linter would presumably use the compiler's parser instead.
  • The rules' source: they come from the Roc style guide in roc-apps, docs/roc-style.md.

If he wants a fourth that's mostly heuristics rather than structure, there's name_hunt.shale (681 lines). It applies five naming heuristics and reports each finding as a question.

From my Claude:

Yes. Shale uses the Roc compiler's own parser, built straight from its sources, but not inside Shale itself. It goes through a small separate program:

  • roc-ast (in roc-webbox, tools/roc_ast) is about one file of Zig. It pulls roc-lang/roc in as a Zig package at a pinned commit, links the compiler's own parse module, and prints each file's syntax tree with the compiler's own debug printer (AST.toSExprStr).
  • Shale runs that program and reads its printed tree. roc_tree turns the text back into nodes. So the parse is exactly the compiler's; only the hand-over is text.

Why it isn't linked into Shale:

  1. Zig versions: Roc's build needs exactly Zig 0.16 (roc-ast's build refuses anything else), while Shale is built with our patched Zig 0.17. They can't be one build today.
  2. Dependencies: pulling the whole Roc compiler into Shale's build would make every Shale build depend on Roc. Our rule is to avoid dependencies, and a separate program keeps Shale independent.
  3. Pinning: the parser has to match the Roc a project is built with. A separate program can be pinned and rebuilt on its own schedule.

What it costs us:

  • The text hand-over breaks on some shapes. The two roc_tree bugs we found today are exactly that: Shale's reader of the printed tree trips on two shapes the printer emits.
  • The pin has drifted. roc-ast's parser is from the 2026-10-09 nightly (258ab27), pinned by roc-webbox, while roc-chat now builds with the 2026-10-30 nightly. Syntax that changed in those three weeks could be misread by the linters. Rebuilding roc-ast at roc-chat's pin, or giving roc-ast its own roc-version, would close that gap.

For notramo, this is the real case for native-Roc linters: if Roc ever exposes its parser to Roc code, a linter gets the tree as data, with no text to re-parse and no version to drift.
Executive summary: I think notramo should explore using compiler sources directly. The reasons I don't are related to some Steve-specific factors related to my ecosystem of Roc apps.

I have a linter written in Roc. It's called roc-policy any is configurable, with some additional test inventory and execution features. It checks conventions and some random things the compiler doesn’t cover.

  • Compiler and dependencies: enforce compiler pins and exact dependency values in Roc headers.
  • Import boundaries: flag forbidden imports.
  • Public documentation: require ## comments for public definitions.
  • Spelling: find known typos in comments, identifiers, strings and prose. (vendors the typos dictionary)
  • Language conventions: flag explicitly configured phrases, optionally suggesting replacements.

The confgiguration lives in Blueprint.roc. You write profiles, select files with globs, set warning/error levels, and declare exceptions etc. 

roc-policy check --root .
roc-policy check --root . --format json
roc-policy explain-config --root . --path package/Thing.roc

Download it from a release https://github.com/lukewilliamboswell/roc-automation/releases/tag/tools-0.8.0

The recent Gergely interview with the Google tooling guy made me curious about declarative code mods for Roc. Something like the roc tooling linter or elm-review, but more focused on applying some kind of structured edit across a codebase. Like "replace all usages of this method with this other one in this particular way".

@Dan G Knutson That's what shale is doing: structured edits. Shale reads the AST to find the structural changes it needs to make, using the AST to determine the structure and to know where the tokens are in the file. And then it uses primitives like replace() to edit the file.

Just to be clear, Shale doesn't have any elegant syntax that is specific to refactoring. Every refactoring just has a concrete program that walks the AST and looks for things. For example, let's say I wanted to flag any potential call stack that was more than N deep. In Shale, just as I would in any other mainstream programming language, I walk the AST, only look at function-call nodes, and increment the count as I walk down the tree.
